overview: WasteCo Group is New Zealand's only NZX-listed waste solutions and industrial services provider, offering waste collection and recycling, road/street sweeping, and industrial cleaning services to households, businesses, healthcare providers, and local councils nationwide. The company was formed via a December 2022 reverse takeover of the operating WasteCo Holdings business into the NZX-listed shell Goodwood Capital Limited, and has grown rapidly since through acquisitions (notably Cleanways in FY2024 and Civic Waste in November 2024), expanding from a South Island regional operator into a business with a presence across Auckland, Hamilton, Wellington, Nelson/Marlborough, Canterbury, South Canterbury, Otago and Southland. It remains loss-making every year since listing and entered FY2027 carrying a highly leveraged balance sheet and a going-concern qualification.

business_model.summary: WasteCo earns revenue from three operating segments — waste collection & recycling, sweeping services, and industrial cleaning — sold to councils, healthcare providers, infrastructure operators and commercial/industrial customers. More than 45% of group revenue comes from long-term contracts (multi-year council and commercial agreements), giving a partially recurring, partially contracted revenue base, though customer concentration is meaningful (top two customers were ~24% of FY2026 revenue). Growth has been a mix of organic contract wins (e.g. the incoming nine-year, ~NZ$40m Ashburton District Council solid waste contract starting FY2027) and debt/equity-funded acquisitions that have driven most of the topline growth since FY2023.
business_model.customer_type: B2B and B2G — local/regional councils, healthcare and infrastructure operators, commercial and industrial clients, plus some residential collection; not a mass-market B2C business
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand; South Island historically core (Canterbury, Otago, Southland, Nelson/Marlborough) with North Island exposure (Auckland, Hamilton, Wellington) added via the December 2024 Civic Waste acquisition

main_competitors: WM New Zealand (formerly Waste Management NZ)
Smaller regional/independent waste and sweeping operators
competitive_position.market_position: Small-cap, sub-scale challenger in a market dominated by two much larger, well-capitalised operators (WM New Zealand and EnviroWaste/EnviroNZ); WasteCo differentiates via regional density in the South Island, sweeping services, and a niche Medical & Quarantine (M&Q) waste capability where it is one of only two operators of M&Q processing facilities in NZ

moat_factors.description: Multi-year contracts (>45% of revenue) create switching costs and revenue visibility, though contracts are periodically re-tendered and can be lost or won competitively (as with Ashburton)
One of only two NZ operators of M&Q processing facilities; a specialised, harder-to-replicate capability with growth potential (Cromwell transfer facility, Queenstown Airport contract)

Multi-region footprint and vertically integrated collection/processing (e.g. new Porirua construction & demolition sorting facility) support local economies of scale, but the network was built quickly via acquisition and is not yet efficiently integrated
Dwarfed in scale, balance-sheet strength and operating efficiency by WM New Zealand and EnviroWaste; NZX listing provides capital-markets access but not an operating advantage

weaknesses: Sub-scale relative to the two dominant national operators, limiting pricing power and cost leverage
Ageing, acquired fleet with high operating and maintenance costs and low utilisation
Integration of multiple acquisitions (Cleanways, Civic Waste, others) has not delivered promised synergies; duplicated overheads and fragmented procurement persisted into FY2026
High customer concentration risk with top-two customers ~24% of FY2026 revenue
Weak balance sheet materially constrains competitive flexibility (bidding for new contracts, fleet capex) relative to better-capitalised rivals

growth_drivers: Ashburton District Council contract: nine-year, ~NZ$40m solid waste/kerbside/FOGO contract commencing FY2027, WasteCo's largest single council win to date

Expansion of the Medical & Quarantine waste division, which management flags as having 'significant growth potential', supported by new Cromwell transfer facility and Queenstown International Airport contract
New Porirua City Council construction & demolition (C&D) waste sorting facility (>30,000 tonnes/year capacity), diversifying into landfill-diversion infrastructure
Nationwide tender capability unlocked by the Civic Waste acquisition, allowing WasteCo to bid for national (not just regional) waste contracts
Ongoing restructuring/cost-out program (centralised procurement, in-housing of HR/professional services, national fleet management) targeted to deliver 'significant annualised savings' from H1 FY2027

Disciplined M&A pipeline in a fragmented industry, with management citing valuation arbitrage between private and listed multiples and infrastructure-investor interest in defensive waste-sector earnings
Structural, government-driven waste levy increases pushing volumes toward diversion/recycling services WasteCo can provide, rather than landfill

business.risk: Two fatal incidents and an active WorkSafe prosecution
business.description: WorkSafe charged WasteCo NZ Ltd under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 (max penalty up to NZ$1.5m) over the 2025 death of employee Lynda Kelly at the Te Anau transfer station; a second fatality (Paul Cruse, Cardrona, early 2026) remains under police investigation. Reputational, legal, contract-tender and insurance implications are material for a company whose core customers are risk-averse councils and healthcare providers
Two customers each contributed >10% of FY2026 revenue (NZ$9.1m and NZ$7.8m combined ~24% of revenue); loss or repricing of either would be material

Management's own FY26 report catalogues systemic operational failures — fragmented procurement, ageing fleet, poor asset utilisation, duplicated overheads, underperforming/loss-making business units — following rapid, debt-funded acquisition growth since listing

CEO David Peterson resigned effective June 2025; Chair Roger Gower has served as Interim CEO since, alongside multiple board resignations (Shane Edmond, Rodney Malam, James Redmayne) within the last 12 months, breaching NZX Code recommendations on independent chair/CEO separation and board independence

Well-capitalised international and established domestic operators (WM New Zealand, EnviroWaste/EnviroNZ) compete for the same council and commercial contracts where scale and balance-sheet strength increasingly matter

financial.description: FY2026 accounts disclose a going-concern material uncertainty: shareholders' equity collapsed to NZ$3.2m (from NZ$15.3m) against total debt of ~NZ$58.1m (borrowings NZ$40.1m plus lease liabilities ~NZ$18.0m); negative working capital of NZ$28.7m; the Group breached (or was likely to breach) equity and leverage covenants with Kiwibank at 31 March 2026, received only a conditional waiver dated the balance date itself, and as a result NZ$26.7m of borrowings (up from NZ$8.7m a year earlier) were reclassified from non-current to current. This is WasteCo's second disclosed covenant issue — it also breached interest cover/leverage covenants with Kiwibank in September 2024, sending the share price down ~13% at the time. Covenant renegotiation with Kiwibank was still in progress as of the FY26 signing date (targeted resolution by 29 June 2026)

A NZ$15.4m Kiwibank asset-finance facility matures 30 May 2027 and must be rolled over or refinanced; the going-concern note explicitly flags this as a key uncertainty. A planned NZ$10m receivables-backed financing facility with Pacific Finance Limited was only provisionally approved (20 May 2026) and not yet executed at signing

financial.risk: High finance costs eroding EBITDA gains
financial.description: Finance costs were NZ$5.5m in FY2026 (NZ$5.1m FY2025) against Operating EBITDA of NZ$5.85m (FY2025 NZ$4.64m) — interest expense consumes almost all EBITDA, and rising secured/convertible-note debt (weighted convertible-note effective rates of 14–18%) is expensive

Empire Waste Technology Limited (related party via director Simon Herbert) holds NZ$15m of convertible notes that could convert into up to 750 million shares — up to 40.6% of the fully diluted register — a major latent dilution and control-concentration risk for existing minority holders

financial.risk: Persistent net losses / share-based equity erosion
financial.description: Loss-making every year since the FY2023 reverse listing (loss per share -NZ$0.0035 to -NZ$0.011); accumulated losses have driven retained earnings to -NZ$26.4m and shrunk net assets to NZ$3.2m at FY2026

regulatory.risk: Rising national waste disposal levy and compliance costs
regulatory.description: Government levy increases (municipal landfill levy reached NZ$65/tonne from 1 July 2025, having risen from lower levels through 2024, with further scheduled increases to 2027) raise operating costs and compliance/reporting burden across the industry, even as they create some diversion-related revenue opportunity

Active WorkSafe prosecution and police investigation into workplace fatalities carry potential fines, adverse findings, and could affect the company's ability to win or retain council tenders that increasingly weight H&S performance

WasteCo does not comply with several NZX Corporate Governance Code recommendations (majority-independent board, independent chair, chair/CEO separation, audit-committee composition), disclosed as 'comply or explain' departures

macro.description: Heavily indebted with variable-rate bank facilities (overdraft, asset finance at cost-of-funds-plus-margin) — elevated for-longer NZ interest rates directly pressure an already thin interest-cover position

macro.risk: Fuel, labour and landfill cost inflation
macro.description: Management explicitly cites rising fuel, labour and landfill levy costs pressuring sector margins

macro.risk: Economic cyclicality of commercial/industrial waste volumes
macro.description: Council and residential waste demand is largely non-discretionary/essential, but commercial and industrial cleaning volumes can soften in a slowing economy, and construction & demolition waste is tied to building activity

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The NZ waste services sector is viewed by management and industry commentary as stable and essential (demand largely inelastic to the economic cycle), but structurally more challenging: increasing waste levies, stricter reporting/compliance requirements, and rising input costs (fuel, labour, landfill) are compressing margins industry-wide, while scale, efficient operations and long-term contracts are becoming more important competitive differentiators, favouring the two large incumbents
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate — collection/council revenue is largely non-discretionary, but sweeping, industrial cleaning and construction & demolition waste volumes have some sensitivity to commercial activity and construction cycles
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — the balance sheet carries ~NZ$40m of borrowings (bank overdraft, asset finance, convertible notes) plus ~NZ$18m of lease liabilities at generally variable or high fixed rates (asset finance ~7.2% weighted average FY26; convertible notes effective rates of 14–18%), so financing costs are a first-order determinant of profitability and covenant headroom
key_input_costs: Government waste disposal levy per tonne

recent_developments.event: FY2026 annual report (year ended 31 March 2026) discloses a going-concern material uncertainty, a covenant breach/conditional waiver with Kiwibank at year-end, and reclassification of NZ$26.7m of borrowings to current liabilities; net loss widened to NZ$12.35m (FY2025: NZ$9.85m) despite revenue growth to NZ$70.2m (FY2025: NZ$56.4m)

WorkSafe formally charged WasteCo NZ Limited under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 over the April/May 2025 death of employee Lynda Kelly at the Te Anau transfer station (maximum penalty up to NZ$1.5m)
A second employee/contractor fatality (Paul Cruse) occurred in a Cardrona road accident, remaining under active police investigation

Two non-independent directors, Rodney Malam and James Redmayne, resigned from the Board (1 May and 25 May 2026 respectively); independent director Shane Edmond had already resigned 28 February 2026; new independent director Neil McAra appointed 1 March 2026
Won and is preparing to mobilise the nine-year, ~NZ$40m Ashburton District Council solid waste contract (kerbside rubbish, recycling and new FOGO service), commencing FY2027

CEO David Peterson resigned effective end of June 2025 (relocating to Australia); Chair Roger Gower has since served as Interim CEO, a governance departure from NZX Code recommendations on chair/CEO separation

Issued an additional NZ$1m unsecured convertible note (combined with renewal of an existing NZ$1m note) to a wholesale investor, extending maturity to October 2027 at 10% cash interest / 18% effective rate
Sold a non-core mowing business (acquired via the Cleanways acquisition) that had been held for sale since FY2025

Committed ~NZ$1.75m to a Health & Safety systems reset (new leadership, digital training platform, Safer Driving Strategy) and incurred NZ$1.35m of restructuring costs simplifying the business post rapid acquisition growth
(Prior period) WasteCo breached interest cover and leverage covenants with Kiwibank; shares fell ~13% on disclosure — establishing a pattern of recurring covenant stress

items.target: Further debt reduction planned during FY27 (FY26 repaid NZ$7.3m of debt principal)
items.notes: No numeric FY27 target disclosed; framed qualitatively as a continuing priority alongside covenant renegotiation with Kiwibank (targeted resolution by 29 June 2026)

items.target: 'Significant annualised savings' from restructuring and in-housing of professional/HR services
items.notes: No specific dollar figure quantified in the annual report

items.target: Commence the ~NZ$40m, nine-year Ashburton District Council solid waste contract
items.period: October 2026 (per annual report; council materials cite 1 September 2026 start)
items.notes: Contract flagged in both the FY2025 and FY2026 annual reports as a confirmed win

items.target: Deliver 'better results' / 'a stronger performance' for FY2027 and subsequent years
items.notes: Chair & Interim CEO's letter is explicitly qualitative — no revenue, EBITDA, or loss target was quantified for FY2027 in the annual report

guidance.management_commentary: Chair & Interim CEO Roger Gower described FY2026 as 'a disappointing year for WasteCo, both operationally and financially,' attributing the loss to high financing costs, low asset utilisation, rising fleet/operating costs, duplicated overheads and one-off restructuring/Health & Safety reset costs layered on an underperforming core business. He stated the returns on remediation initiatives 'will take time to be reflected in our financial performance' but expressed confidence in improvement 'in the current financial year' (FY2027), while acknowledging 'we know there is still a lot of work to do.' No formal quantitative guidance (revenue, EBITDA or loss range) was issued for FY2027.

bull_case: Revenue has grown consistently (NZ$34.4m FY2023 to NZ$70.2m FY2026, ~+104% over three years) and Operating EBITDA has also grown into FY2026 (NZ$5.85m vs a FY2024 trough of NZ$3.37m), giving some evidence the underlying businesses generate cash even while net losses persist

The newly won ~NZ$40m, nine-year Ashburton District Council contract and continued expansion of the niche, higher-margin Medical & Quarantine waste business provide visible, contracted revenue growth into FY2027 without further M&A

Management has explicitly acknowledged the operational failures (fragmented procurement, ageing fleet, duplicated overheads) and has a concrete, funded cost-out and fleet-simplification plan that, if executed, could meaningfully improve margins from a low base

The waste levy regime and essential-service nature of council/collection contracts provide structural, non-discretionary demand and long contract durations (>45% of revenue under long-term agreements) that support revenue visibility once the balance sheet is stabilised

A fragmented NZ waste industry with disciplined consolidation opportunities and reported infrastructure-investor interest in the sector could eventually support a re-rating or a takeout, particularly if scale operators such as WM New Zealand or EnviroNZ see value in WasteCo's contracted revenue base
bear_case: Explicit going-concern material uncertainty: equity has fallen to just NZ$3.2m against ~NZ$58m of total debt/lease liabilities, negative working capital of NZ$28.7m, and covenant compliance with Kiwibank was only conditionally waived at year-end and remained under renegotiation as the accounts were signed — a genuine risk of equity being wiped out or heavily diluted in a restructuring or forced refinancing

Active WorkSafe prosecution (max fine NZ$1.5m) and a second fatality under police investigation create legal, reputational, and potential contract-loss risk for a company whose customers are councils and healthcare providers that screen heavily on safety record

Persistent, widening net losses every year since the FY2023 reverse listing (loss grew to NZ$12.35m in FY2026 from NZ$9.85m in FY2025) despite revenue growth, indicating a structurally uneconomic cost base relative to scale, not just one-off items

Up to 750 million shares of latent dilution from the Empire Waste Technology convertible notes (up to 40.6% of the fully diluted register) sit alongside a leadership vacuum (interim, non-independent CEO/Chair combined role, multiple recent board resignations) that raises execution and governance risk

Sub-scale versus WM New Zealand and EnviroWaste/EnviroNZ leaves WasteCo structurally disadvantaged on cost per tonne, fleet utilisation and access to capital — a disadvantage that widens, not narrows, in a rising-rate, rising-levy environment, and management's own FY26 letter confirms the business has not yet achieved the promised acquisition synergies
